newsitem.title: HONG KONG: HK's future chamber agrees on law-making plan.
newsitem.headline: HK's future chamber agrees on law-making plan.

text.p: Future Hong Kong lawmakers on Saturday agreed on a formula to enact laws for the territory before Britain hands it back to China at midnight Jun 30.

The 60-member provisional legislature convened in China's southern Shenzhen city to decide on the format, which would enable them to pass bills, including those to dilute existing Hong Kong laws protecting civil liberties and freedoms.
The interim council, crafted by China in December, agreed that all three readings of bills will be over before July 1.
The bills would then be confirmed on July 1, the local Cable television station reported.
The decision was reached despite threats by the pro-democracy camp to sue the chamber if it passes any laws, holds meetings or opens offices on Hong Kong soil before July 1.

Hong Kong democrats regard the interim chamber, which China intends to put in place of the existing elected legislature upon the handover, as a breach of the territory's post-handover constitution and Sino-British handover treaties on Hong Kong.
The interim chamber had met in late March to discuss the law-making format but no agreement was reached.

Earlier, pro-democracy activists sent a banner attached to dozens of helium-filled balloons drifting to China to protest against the provisional legislature and its attempts to pass laws for the territory.
Rita Fan, president of the provisional legislature, said she was not worried about any potential legal challenge.

"I feel relatively easy about it. Hong Kong is a free society. Anyone who wishes to go to court and accuse anyone of doing anything can do so within the realms of the law," she said on Radio Television Hong Kong.
